messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus Webb: A Clinical Vignette

Marcus Webb was fifty-three when he finally made the call to schedule a trauma-focused therapy appointment, though the event that brought him to that decision had occurred fourteen years earlier, during a conference in a mid-sized city where he had traveled for his work as a social worker specializing in adolescent mental health. He had been attending a continuing education seminar in a hotel near downtown, and after the final afternoon session, he'd decided to take a shortcut through the basement corridor to reach the parking garage rather than navigate the crowded lobby. The corridor was poorly lit, lined with mechanical equipment and storage closets. A man had emerged from behind a utility door—someone Marcus had never seen before—and forced him into an adjacent room, locking the door behind them. What happened in those minutes felt, in Marcus's recollection, like it lasted hours. The assailant had been methodical and violent. Afterward, Marcus had dressed in silence, driven home in a state of dissociation, and told his wife, Patricia, only that he'd had a panic attack at the conference and wanted to leave early.

For years, Marcus had believed he was managing. He returned to work, continued his caseload, attended supervision. But the management was a careful architecture of avoidance that had slowly reshaped his life. He could not bring himself to enter basement parking areas anymore; he now parked on street level, often paying premium rates, rather than descend into those enclosed, dimly lit spaces where his mind insisted danger lurked. Hotel corridors became sources of profound anxiety. He had begun to avoid professional conferences altogether, telling colleagues that budget constraints or scheduling conflicts made attendance impossible. When he did travel for work, he insisted on rooms on upper floors and would not use interior hallways if he could avoid them. The avoidance had cost him—a promotion two years ago had required willingness to present at national conferences, and his reluctance had made him seem uncommitted to career advancement.

What Marcus had never told anyone, not even Patricia, was the way his mind had turned toward revenge. In the quiet hours before sleep, he constructed elaborate scenarios in which he encountered the man again, in which he was stronger, faster, more prepared. He imagined confrontations that never occurred, rehearsed violence he would never enact. These ruminations were exhausting and shameful in themselves—he was a mental health professional who spent his days teaching adolescents healthy coping strategies, yet he spent his nights fantasizing about hurting someone. He tried to push the thoughts away, to redirect his attention to his wife or to work, but the effort of suppression only seemed to make them more insistent, more vivid.

The memory itself had become fragmented in a way that troubled him. He could recall the sequence of events with terrible clarity—the sound of the door locking, the smell of the room, the specific words the man had spoken—yet when he tried to articulate any of it to anyone, the words simply would not come. His mouth would go dry. His throat would close. It was as if his body refused to translate the experience into language. When the memory surfaced unbidden, which it did with increasing frequency over the past year, it returned not as narrative but as pure sensation: the terror he had felt in that moment, immediate and undiminished by time, flooded through him as if he were still trapped there.

His vigilance had become a constant background hum to his existence. He checked behind him when walking through the hallways of his office building. He positioned himself in rooms so that he could see the door. When a client session ran over time, when traffic delayed his commute, when anything disrupted the expected timeline of his day, his mind immediately generated the worst possible explanation—something had gone wrong, something bad was happening, danger was imminent. Patricia had begun to notice his distraction, his irritability, the way he would tense when she suggested they take a weekend trip or visit friends in unfamiliar neighborhoods. He could not explain to her why the unpredictability of new places felt genuinely dangerous to him, why he needed to know the layout, the exits, the potential threats before he could feel even remotely safe.

What finally moved him to seek help was not insight but exhaustion. He was tired of the constant surveillance of his own environment, tired of the thoughts he could not stop, tired of the shame that accompanied both the memory and his ruminations about revenge. He called a trauma-specialized therapist on a Tuesday morning, his voice steady but his hands trembling as he scheduled the first appointment. He did not yet believe that anything could truly change, but he had begun to understand that the architecture of avoidance that had once felt protective was now the structure imprisoning him.
